idiom_name: index signature (Record<string, unknown>) + Proxy for undeclared names
implementation_notes: TypeScript expresses the pattern in the type system: an index signature describes the case where you do not know all property names ahead of time but do know the shape of the values, Record<string, unknown> is its utility-type form, and readonly or template-literal index signatures narrow which names are admissible. At runtime the object is a JavaScript property bag, or a Proxy when names must be intercepted and validated, while mapped types and indexed access types build typed views over known keys. The declaration is absorbed by the language, but no checker can verify a name computed at runtime, so noUncheckedIndexedAccess and boundary validation are the countermeasures.
pitfalls: An index signature widens: every declared member must be assignable to the index type, and with noUncheckedIndexedAccess off (the default) a lookup is typed as present although the key may be missing - turn the flag on or add | undefined explicitly.
Types do not exist at runtime: names that come from data bypass the checker entirely, so validate keys and values at the boundary and keep a runtime allow-list for untrusted input.

noPropertyAccessFromIndexSignature forces bracket syntax for index-signature members, and symbol-named properties are not covered by a string index signature - discovery must use Reflect.ownKeys()/Object.getOwnPropertySymbols() when symbols are admitted.
